```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.align = "center"
)
has_gt <- requireNamespace("gt", quietly = TRUE)
```

Most cohort studies and trials report how a starting population was whittled
down to the analysed cohort: who was assessed, who was excluded and why, and
how many were left at each stage. That record usually ends up scattered
across `filter()` calls, hand-counted tables and a flow diagram drawn in
PowerPoint, and the three drift apart as the analysis changes.

cohortflow keeps a single record. You write the eligibility criteria once as
a pipeline, apply it to your data, and derive the final cohort, the excluded
rows, the attrition table and the CONSORT diagram from the same object, so
they always agree.

```{r setup}
library(cohortflow)
```

## Example data

The package ships with generators for four common trial designs. Here we use
a two-arm parallel-group randomised trial with 300 people assessed for
eligibility. Like real data, it is untidy: some ages are missing, some
people failed screening or never consented, and some withdrew.

```{r}
dat <- mock_parallel_rct(n_participants = 300, seed = 2024)
dat
```

## 1. Define the criteria

A pipeline starts with `cf_criteria()`, and each step is added with a pipe.
`include()` keeps the rows where its condition is `TRUE`; `exclude()` drops
the rows where its condition is `TRUE`. Each step has a `label` for
reporting, and steps can share a `category` so they are reported together.

`randomise()` removes nobody. It marks the point at which people were
allocated, so later reports can show what happened in each arm afterwards.

```{r}
crit <- cf_criteria() |>
  include(~ !is.na(age), label = "Age recorded", reason = "Age missing", category = "Age") |>
  include(~ age >= 18, label = "Aged 18 or over", reason = "Under 18", category = "Age") |>
  include(~ eligible_screen, label = "Passed screening", reason = "Failed screening") |>
  include(~ !is.na(consent_date), label = "Consented", reason = "Did not consent") |>
  randomise(by = "participant_id", arms = "arm") |>
  exclude(~ withdrew, label = "Withdrew consent") |>
  include(~ baseline_complete, label = "Baseline complete", reason = "Baseline incomplete")

crit
```

In the printout, `[+]` marks an inclusion step, `[-]` an exclusion and `[R]`
the randomisation point. `[~]` means the condition is a formula. The
[Writing criteria](writing-criteria.html) article covers every step type.

## 2. Apply them

`apply_criteria()` runs the steps in order. Each step sees only the rows that
survived the steps before it. `id` names the column that identifies a row.

```{r}
flow <- apply_criteria(dat, crit, id = "participant_id")
flow
```

The result is a `cf_flow`: the original data plus a record of which rows
each step removed. Everything below is read from it.

## 3. Get the cohort

`cohort()` returns the rows that passed every step, and `excluded()` returns
the rows that were removed, labelled with the step that removed them:

```{r}
final <- cohort(flow)
nrow(final)

removed <- excluded(flow)
table(removed$cf_label)
```

Both take a step selector (a step number, a label or a category), so you can
also get the cohort as it stood at an earlier point. For example, here is
everyone who was randomised:

```{r}
nrow(cohort(flow, at = "Consented"))
```

## 4. Attrition table

`as_attrition_tibble()` returns the counts as a plain data frame, ready for
your own formatting or further calculation:

```{r}
as_attrition_tibble(flow)
```

`as_attrition_table()` formats the same data with flextable (the default,
best for Word), gt or huxtable. Steps that share a category are grouped
under one heading, and because there is a `randomise()` step, the final row
is broken out by arm.

```{r, eval = has_gt}
as_attrition_table(flow, backend = "gt")
```

The [Attrition tables](https://mattmoo.github.io/cohortflow/articles/attrition-tables.html) article covers
grouped tables, shading and the other backends.

## 5. CONSORT flow diagram

`as_consort_diagram()` draws the flow. Up to the randomisation box there is
one shared trunk. After it, each arm gets its own column, so post-allocation
losses are reported separately for each arm, as CONSORT asks.

```{r, fig.width = 10.2, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "CONSORT flow diagram. 300 people were assessed; 105 were excluded at six steps; after randomisation the Control and Intervention arms finish with 107 and 88."}
diagram <- as_consort_diagram(flow)
diagram
```

Each main box shows how many people remain after a step, and each side box
how many that step removed, each beside text that describes those people.
An inclusion step's label ("Passed screening") goes on the main box and its
`reason` ("Failed screening") on the side box. An exclusion step's label
("Withdrew consent") goes on the side box, and the main box below it reads
"Remaining". A category's side box lists the reason for each of its steps
(here, *Age*).

The diagram is a ggplot. Save it for a manuscript with
`save_consort_diagram()`, which picks the format from the file extension and
sizes the page so the text fits its boxes:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
save_consort_diagram(diagram, "consort.pdf")
save_consort_diagram(diagram, "consort.png", dpi = 300)
```

The [CONSORT diagrams](https://mattmoo.github.io/cohortflow/articles/consort-diagrams.html) article covers
styling and other trial designs.

## 6. Who was excluded?

Reviewers often ask whether exclusions changed the make-up of the cohort.
`as_characteristics_table()` summarises chosen variables at every step, in
one column per step:

```{r, eval = has_gt}
as_characteristics_table(
  flow,
  vars = c("age", "sex"),
  steps = list(0, "Consented", "Baseline complete"),
  var_labels = c(age = "Age, years", sex = "Sex"),
  backend = "gt"
)
```

Use `excluded = TRUE` to describe the people removed at each step instead.
The [Describing who was excluded](https://mattmoo.github.io/cohortflow/articles/describing-exclusions.html)
article covers this and overlapping exclusion reasons.

> **Missing values.** A condition that gives `NA` is treated differently by
> the two step types. `include(~ age >= 18)` *removes* a row with a missing
> age; `exclude(~ age < 18)` *keeps* it. Here 15 people have no recorded age,
> so the choice changes the denominator. This pipeline makes the choice
> visible with a separate "Age recorded" step. See [Missing
> values](writing-criteria.html#missing-values) for a worked example.

## 7. Writing it up

The methods section usually describes the same flow in words.
`as_narrative()` writes that paragraph from the flow, so its numbers match
the table and the diagram. Each step is described by its `reason`, and after
randomisation each sentence gives the counts for each arm:

```{r}
as_narrative(flow)
```

Use `style = "bullets"` to get one sentence per line, which is easier to
edit into a draft. Set `unit` to the noun your study counts (for example
"patients"). Read the text through and adapt it to the journal's style.

```{r}
as_narrative(flow, style = "bullets", unit = "people")
```

## 8. Save the criteria

A criteria pipeline can be written to YAML and read back, so the exact
definitions can be kept under version control, shared with collaborators or
attached to a protocol:

```{r}
yml <- export_criteria(crit)
cat(yml)

identical(
  as_attrition_tibble(apply_criteria(dat, import_criteria(text = yml), id = "participant_id")),
  as_attrition_tibble(flow)
)
```

Pass `path =` to `export_criteria()` and `import_criteria()` to write and
read a file instead.
